extraction.name: ACL OCL Corpus: Advancing Open Science in Computational Linguistics
extraction.description: ACL OCL is a scholarly corpus derived from the ACL Anthology to assist Open scientific research in the Computational Linguistics domain. Integrating and enhancing previous versions of the ACL Anthology, the ACL OCL contributes metadata, PDF files, citation graphs, and additional structured full texts with sections, figures, and links to a large knowledge resource (Semantic Scholar). The ACL OCL spans seven decades, containing 73K papers, alongside 210K figures. It is used to observe trends in computational linguistics, for example, detecting paper topics with a supervised neural model.
extraction.creator: Shaurya Rohatgi, Yanxia Qin, Benjamin Aw, Niranjana Unnithan, Min-Yen Kan
extraction.citeAs: Shaurya Rohatgi, Yanxia Qin, Benjamin Aw, Niranjana Unnithan, and Min-Yen Kan. The ACL OCL Corpus: Advancing Open Science in Computational Linguistics. arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.14996, 2023.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The data collection process involves designing crawlers to fetch all PDF documents and metadata from the ACL Anthology website. Meta information from the website is prioritized for accuracy. PDF files longer than 50 pages, which are mostly conference volume introductions or handbooks, are removed. This process resulted in 73,285 conference journal and workshop papers in the CL domain.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Missing sections (19 sections not detected from 21 scientific papers), footnote numbers concatenated to the body text (25 footnotes missing out of 92), 28.78% (19/66) figures not detected, 31.58% (24/76) tables not detected, and 46.06% (35/76) tables detected with either wrong contents or titles. Incorrect metadata such as author names exceeding three tokens is a common issue, which is addressed by using metadata from ACL Anthology.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: PDF documents and metadata from the ACL Anthology website (aclanthology.org).
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: PDF files longer than 50 pages are removed. The OCL corpus is linked with the Semantic Scholar Academic Graph (S2AG) using its Graph API to fetch additional information such as citation data. Citation networks are constructed using in-degree (internal citations within OCL) and citationCount (external citations from S2AG).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: PDF files are passed through a full-text extraction process using GROBID. Figures and tables are extracted from PDF files using PDFFigures. Language detection is performed using a public language detection toolkit (Shuyo, 2010) with the title and abstract as inputs. Model-predicted CL topics are added.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A subset of 2,545 scientific papers with ground truth topic labels was curated by crawling published papers and their topics from several online held CL conferences (ACL 2020, EMNLP 2020, ACL-IJCNLP 2021, EACL 2021, NAACL 2021) between 2020 and 2022. These topics are taken from the submission topics of the ACL conferences, representing 21 objective topics.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The topic data curation involved aligning crawled papers with the ACL OCL data. The dataset was split into 80% training (2,036 papers) and 20% test (509 papers) using 5-fold cross-validation, balanced in each topic. Evaluation metrics used were Macro F1, Weighted F1, and Accuracy (Micro F1).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: GROBID (for full-text extraction), PDFFigures (for figure and table extraction), a public language detection toolkit (Shuyo, 2010), BART-large-MNLI (for NLI-based zero-shot and fine-tuned semi-supervised topic classification), TF-IDF and Yake! (for keyword extraction in supervised topic classification), SciBERT and SPECTER (for PLM-based supervised topic classification).
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset undergoes annual updates, during which papers recently added to the ACL Anthology are downloaded and processed. New additions are identified by monitoring changes in URLs. In the future, the plan is to update OCL annually to keep it alive. The ultimate solution is to provide full-text extraction and information extraction APIs to ACL Anthology, thus hosting the OCL data on ACL Anthology itself.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Building scholarly corpora for open research accelerates scientific progress and promotes reproducibility. The ACL OCL provides accessible and standardized data resources for researchers. It enables observing trends in computational linguistics, such as the emergence of new topics like 'Ethics' and the resurgence of 'Natural Language Generation'. It can facilitate the construction of a knowledge graph, enabling a more intelligent academic search engine beyond keyword matching.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The linguistic distribution shows English as the most dominant language, with other languages like Latin and Gujarati also present. Prior research indicates that numerous low-resource languages remain underrepresented and show significant disparity in coverage. The accuracy of topic prediction for top-cited papers (87%) is higher than the general test set accuracy (69%) due to a bias in the distribution of top-cited papers towards dominant topics (e.g., Machine Translation).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The OCL corpus is a small-scale collection focusing specifically on peer-reviewed and open-access CL papers, not a comprehensive corpus like S2ORC, as it does not include sources beyond the ACL Anthology. Expansion to include CL papers on arXiv (e.g., cs.CL) is a future consideration, but filtering low-quality arXiv papers is a challenge. Due to budget constraints, only open-source PDF2text toolkits were considered, acknowledging that paid services might yield higher quality. The OCL corpus is an unlabeled resource, lacking annotations for specific tasks that require labels.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning. The dataset is designed to assist Open scientific research in Computational Linguistics. Specific use cases include: observing trends in computational linguistics (e.g., temporal topic trends), document-level information extraction tasks, section-wise tasks (e.g., related work generation, fine-grained linguistic analyses), multimodal research (e.g., figure caption generation), emerging topic detection, evolution detection of topics, paper-reviewer matching, document-level terminology detection, coreference resolution, pre-training scientific large language models, fine-tuning general LLMs, building scientific assistants, contribution extraction, future work prediction, analysis of generalization ability of NLP models, examining modifications to pre-print versions, analyzing historical language change (e.g., vocabulary change), constructing knowledge graphs, and multimodal research tasks (e.g., summarization integrating text summaries with figures and citation visualizations).
